variants.title: Treat visibility as a lease
variants.context: Receive does not mean complete. A receive leases the message through a visibility timeout; the message is complete only after the consumer’s durable work succeeds and DeleteMessage succeeds with the current receipt handle.
variants.prompt: A worker processes messages from a queue. Put the lease protocol in order.

items.text: Long-poll a bounded batch that can finish within the lease.
Validate the contract before any side effect.
Apply the work with an idempotency key written atomically with the effect.
Extend visibility only while the worker can prove live progress.
Delete with the current receipt handle after success, checking each batch entry.

variants.hint: Deletion is the completion event, and it comes last.
variants.explanation: Receive → validate → apply with key → heartbeat live work → delete the receipt. Batch deletes can fail per entry.

variants.title: Treat visibility as a lease
variants.context: Receive does not mean complete. A receive leases the message through a visibility timeout; the message is complete only after the consumer’s durable work succeeds and DeleteMessage succeeds with the current receipt handle.
variants.prompt: A message needs a long-running job. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Receive a small batch under long polling.
Reject unsupported versions deliberately rather than burning transient retries.
Write the operation key and effect together at the destination.
Call ChangeMessageVisibility while the job is genuinely progressing.
Delete the current receipt once the job’s result is durable.

variants.explanation: Stop extending when the worker loses ownership or cannot prove progress.

variants.title: Treat visibility as a lease
variants.context: Receive does not mean complete. A receive leases the message through a visibility timeout; the message is complete only after the consumer’s durable work succeeds and DeleteMessage succeeds with the current receipt handle.
variants.prompt: A worker crashes mid-batch. Put what happens next in order, from the surviving flow’s view.

items.text: Messages were received and made invisible for the lease period.
Validation had passed for the ones in flight.
Any effect already applied is keyed, so a repeat becomes a no-op.
Nobody extends the lease, so visibility expires.
Another worker receives the same messages and completes with delete.

variants.hint: An expired lease is how the queue recovers from a dead worker.
variants.explanation: Idempotency at the effect boundary makes the redelivery safe.

variants.title: Choose the queue type
variants.context: Standard queues give at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering for independent work. FIFO queues preserve order within a MessageGroupId and suppress duplicate sends by deduplication ID; one hot or blocked group stays serial. Neither makes an external side effect exactly once.
variants.prompt: Thumbnail jobs are independent, duplicates are harmless, and throughput matters most. Which queue?
options: FIFO with a group per job.
optionFeedback: Standard queues fit independent, duplicate-safe work at scale.
One group makes everything serial.
Per-job groups add ordering machinery for nothing.
variants.explanation: Choose Standard when messages can run independently and effects are idempotent.

variants.title: Choose the queue type
variants.context: Standard queues give at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering for independent work. FIFO queues preserve order within a MessageGroupId and suppress duplicate sends by deduplication ID; one hot or blocked group stays serial. Neither makes an external side effect exactly once.
variants.prompt: Events for one account must be processed in order, but accounts are independent. Which queue?
options: FIFO with a single group for all accounts.
optionFeedback: Order within a group; different groups run concurrently.
Standard gives best-effort ordering only.
A single group serializes every account.
variants.hint: What is the smallest entity that needs order?
variants.explanation: Group by the smallest entity that needs order.

variants.title: Choose the queue type
variants.context: Standard queues give at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering for independent work. FIFO queues preserve order within a MessageGroupId and suppress duplicate sends by deduplication ID; one hot or blocked group stays serial. Neither makes an external side effect exactly once.
variants.prompt: A FIFO queue deduplicates sends. Does the consumer’s card charge now happen exactly once?
options: No. Deduplication covers sends; a crash before delete can still repeat processing.
Yes, if the deduplication ID is the charge ID.
optionFeedback: SQS cannot atomically combine DeleteMessage with an external system.
Send dedup is not processing dedup.
The ID stops duplicate sends, not duplicate processing.
variants.explanation: Put the idempotency record and business mutation in one destination transaction when possible.

variants.title: Size for recovery
variants.context: Outage backlog = arrival rate × outage seconds. Catch-up rate = consumer capacity − ongoing arrival rate. Recovery time = outage backlog ÷ catch-up rate. FIFO active workers cannot exceed the number of available message groups.
variants.prompt: Messages arrive at 200 per second and consumers are paused for 600 seconds during a deploy. How large is the outage backlog?

variants.title: Size for recovery
variants.context: Outage backlog = arrival rate × outage seconds. Catch-up rate = consumer capacity − ongoing arrival rate. Recovery time = outage backlog ÷ catch-up rate. FIFO active workers cannot exceed the number of available message groups.
variants.prompt: Consumers sustain 350 per second while arrivals continue at 200 per second. What is the catch-up rate?
variants.explanation: 350 − 200 = 150 messages per second of backlog drained.

mistakes.feedback: Ongoing arrivals consume part of the capacity.

variants.title: Size for recovery
variants.context: Outage backlog = arrival rate × outage seconds. Catch-up rate = consumer capacity − ongoing arrival rate. Recovery time = outage backlog ÷ catch-up rate. FIFO active workers cannot exceed the number of available message groups.
variants.prompt: A 120,000-message backlog drains at 150 per second. How many seconds until it is gone?
variants.explanation: 120,000 ÷ 150 = 800 seconds. Check that against the business deadline before approving the deploy window.

mistakes.feedback: Divide by the catch-up rate of 150, not the full capacity of 350.
Recovery takes longer than the outage when spare capacity is small.

variants.title: Read the failure
variants.context: The most important SQS failure happens after the business operation succeeds but before the receipt is deleted; SQS sees that as unfinished work and redelivers. Visibility must cover processing time, or extend it only for live work.
variants.prompt: The order was written, then DeleteMessage failed. What does SQS do?
options: Redeliver the message after visibility expires; the consumer must treat it as a duplicate.
Move it to the DLQ immediately.
optionFeedback: SQS cannot distinguish a failed delete from a crashed worker.
SQS never saw the completion.
DLQ only after maxReceiveCount.
variants.explanation: Idempotency at the business-effect boundary is what makes this failure harmless.

variants.title: Read the failure
variants.context: The most important SQS failure happens after the business operation succeeds but before the receipt is deleted; SQS sees that as unfinished work and redelivers. Visibility must cover processing time, or extend it only for live work.
variants.prompt: Processing takes 90 seconds but visibility is the 30-second default. What happens?
options: Another consumer receives the same message while the first is still working.
optionFeedback: Extend visibility for live work or shorten the batch.
SQS does not cancel workers.
Extension is the consumer’s job via ChangeMessageVisibility.
variants.explanation: Keep each batch small enough that every message can finish before its lease expires.

variants.title: Read the failure
variants.context: The most important SQS failure happens after the business operation succeeds but before the receipt is deleted; SQS sees that as unfinished work and redelivers. Visibility must cover processing time, or extend it only for live work.
variants.prompt: A message has been received more times than maxReceiveCount. Where does it go?
options: To the dead-letter queue configured by the redrive policy.
Back to the front of the queue.
optionFeedback: A DLQ isolates poison messages from healthy work.
Redrive policy moves it out.
It is preserved for diagnosis, not deleted.
variants.hint: What protects healthy work from an endlessly failing message?
variants.explanation: The DLQ preserves context; someone still has to diagnose and replay.

variants.title: Classify the failure
variants.context: A dead-letter queue isolates messages that exceed maxReceiveCount. Retry timeouts, throttling, and brief outages with backoff and jitter; quarantine invalid schemas and deterministic business-rule failures. The DLQ does not diagnose, repair, or replay by itself.
variants.prompt: A message fails because its schema version is unsupported. Retry with backoff?
options: No. Quarantine it; a deterministic contract error should not consume transient retries.
optionFeedback: Permanent failures go to quarantine unless a code or data change can repair them.
Retrying a deterministic failure just burns the budget.
Infinite retries hide incidents.
variants.hint: Can this failure recover on its own?
variants.explanation: Classify before retrying: transient versus deterministic.

variants.title: Classify the failure
variants.context: A dead-letter queue isolates messages that exceed maxReceiveCount. Retry timeouts, throttling, and brief outages with backoff and jitter; quarantine invalid schemas and deterministic business-rule failures. The DLQ does not diagnose, repair, or replay by itself.
variants.prompt: A downstream API throttles the consumer. Retry?
options: Yes, with backoff and jitter within the receive budget.
optionFeedback: Throttling is transient.
Quarantining transient failures hides capacity problems.
Immediate retries worsen throttling.
variants.explanation: Retry timeouts, throttling, and brief outages with backoff and jitter.

variants.title: Classify the failure
variants.context: A dead-letter queue isolates messages that exceed maxReceiveCount. Retry timeouts, throttling, and brief outages with backoff and jitter; quarantine invalid schemas and deterministic business-rule failures. The DLQ does not diagnose, repair, or replay by itself.
variants.prompt: Does a DLQ repair and replay poison messages by itself?
options: No. It isolates them; diagnosis, repair, and replay are operator workflows.
optionFeedback: Preserve context so someone can repair and replay safely.
Isolation is not repair.
Time does not fix data.
variants.explanation: Quarantine poison messages without hiding incidents: alert on DLQ age and ownership.
